8	NAME
9	====
10	
11	dog — a command-line DNS client
12	
13	
14	SYNOPSIS
15	========
16	
17	`dog [options] [domains...]`
18	
19	**dog** is a command-line DNS client.
20	It has colourful output, supports the DNS-over-TLS and DNS-over-HTTPS protocols, and can emit JSON.
21	
22	
23	EXAMPLES
24	========
25	
26	`dog example.net`
27	: Query the `A` record of a domain using default settings
28	
29	`dog example.net MX`
30	: ...looking up `MX` records instead
31	
32	`dog example.net MX @1.1.1.1`
33	: ...using a specific nameserver instead
34	
35	`dog example.net MX @1.1.1.1 -T`
36	: ...using TCP rather than UDP
37	
38	`dog -q example.net -t MX -n 1.1.1.1 -T`
39	: As above, but using explicit arguments
40	
41	
42	QUERY OPTIONS
43	=============
44	
45	`-q`, `--query=HOST`
46	: Host name or domain name to query.
47	
48	`-t`, `--type=TYPE`
49	: Type of the DNS record being queried (`A`, `MX`, `NS`...)
50	
51	`-n`, `--nameserver=ADDR`
52	: Address of the nameserver to send packets to.
53	
54	`--class=CLASS`
55	: Network class of the DNS record being queried (`IN`, `CH`, `HS`)
56	
57	By default, dog will request A records using the system default resolver. At least one domain name must be passed — dog will not automatically query the root nameservers.
58	
59	Query options passed in using a command-line option, such as ‘`--query lookup.dog`’ or ‘`--type MX`’, or as plain arguments, such as ‘`lookup.dog`’ or ‘`MX`’. dog will make an intelligent guess as to what plain arguments mean (`MX` is quite clearly a type), which makes it easier to compose ad-hoc queries quickly. If precision is desired, use the long-form options.
60	
61	If more than one domain, type, nameserver, or class is specified, dog will perform one query for each combination, and display the combined results in a table. For example, passing three type arguments and two domain name arguments will send six requests.
62	
63	DNS traditionally uses port 53 for both TCP and UDP. To use a resolver with a different port, include the port number after a colon (`:`) in the nameserver address.
64	
65	
66	SENDING OPTIONS
67	===============
68	
69	`--edns=SETTING`
70	: Whether to opt in to DNS. This can be ‘`disable`’, ‘`hide`’, or ‘`show`’.
71	
72	`--txid=NUMBER`
73	: Set the transaction ID to a specific value.
74	
75	`-Z=TWEAKS`
76	: Set uncommon protocol-level tweaks.
77	
78	
79	TRANSPORT OPTIONS
80	=================
81	
82	`-U`, `--udp`
83	: Use the DNS protocol over UDP.
84	
85	`-T`, `--tcp`
86	: Use the DNS protocol over TCP.
87	
88	`-S`, `--tls`
89	: Use the DNS-over-TLS protocol.
90	
91	`-H`, `--https`
92	: Use the DNS-over-HTTPS protocol.
93	
94	By default, dog will use the UDP protocol, automatically re-sending the request using TCP if the response indicates that the message is too large for UDP. Passing `--udp` will only use UDP and will fail in this case; passing `--tcp` will use TCP by default.
95	
96	The DNS-over-TLS (DoT) and DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) protocols are available with the `--tls` and `--https` options. Bear in mind that the system default resolver is unlikely to respond to requests using these protocols.
97	
98	Note that if a hostname or domain name is given as a nameserver, rather than an IP address, the resolution of that host is performed by the operating system, _not_ by dog.
99	
100	Unlike the others, the HTTPS transport type requires an entire URL, complete with protocol, domain name, and path.
101	
102	
103	OUTPUT OPTIONS
104	==============
105	
106	`-1`, `--short`
107	: Short mode: display nothing but the first result.
108	
109	`-J`, `--json`
110	: Display the output as JSON.
111	
112	`--color`, `--colour=WHEN`
113	: When to colourise the output. This can be ‘`always`’, ‘`automatic`’, or ‘`never`’.
114	
115	`--seconds`
116	: Do not format durations as hours and minutes; instead, display them as seconds.
117	
118	`--time`
119	: Print how long the response took to arrive.
120	
121	
122	META OPTIONS
123	============
124	
125	`--help`
126	: Displays an overview of the command-line options.
127	
128	`--version`
129	: Displays the version of dog being invoked.
130	
131	
132	ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES
133	=====================
134	
135	dog responds to the following environment variables:
136	
137	## `DOG_DEBUG`
138	
139	Set this to any non-empty value to have dog emit debugging information to standard error. For more in-depth output, set this to the exact string ‘`trace`’.
140	
141	
142	RECORD TYPES
143	============
144	
145	dog understands and can interpret the following record types:
146	
147	`A`
148	: IPv4 addresses
149	
150	`AAAA`
151	: IPv6 addresses
152	
153	`CAA`
154	: permitted certificate authorities
155	
156	`CNAME`
157	: canonical domain aliases
158	
159	`HINFO`
160	: system information and, sometimes, forbidden request explanations
161	
162	`LOC`
163	: location information
164	
165	`MX`
166	: e-mail server addresses
167	
168	`NAPTR`
169	: DDDS rules
170	
171	`NS`
172	: domain name servers
173	
174	`OPT`
175	: extensions to the DNS protocol
176	
177	`PTR`
178	: pointers to canonical names, usually for reverse lookups
179	
180	`SOA`
181	: administrative information about zones
182	
183	`SRV`
184	: IP addresses with port numbers
185	
186	`SSHFP`
187	: SSH key fingerprints
188	
189	`TLSA`
190	: TLS certificates, public keys, and hashes
191	
192	`TXT`
193	: arbitrary textual information
194	
195	When a response DNS packet contains a record of one of these known types, dog will display it in a table containing the type name and a human-readable summary of its contents.
196	
197	Records with a type number that does not map to any known record type will still be displayed. As they cannot be interpreted, their contents will be displayed as a series of numbers instead.
198	
199	dog also contains a list of record type names that it knows the type number of, but is not able to interpret, such as `IXFR` or `ANY` or `AFSDB`. These are acceptable as command-line arguments, meaning you can send an AFSDB request with ‘`dog AFSDB`’. However, their response contents will still be displayed as numbers. They may be supported in future versions of dog.
200	
201	
202	PROTOCOL TWEAKS
203	===============
204	
205	The `-Z` command-line argument can be used one or more times to set some protocol-level options in the DNS queries that get sent. It accepts the following values:
206	
207	`aa`
208	: Sets the `AA` (Authoritative Answers) bit in the query.
209	
210	`ad`
211	: Sets the `AD` (Authentic Data) bit in the query.
212	
213	`bufsize=NUM`
214	: Sets the UDP payload size field in the OPT field in the query. This has no effect if EDNS is diabled.
215	
216	`cd`
217	: Sets the `CD` (Checking Disabled) bit in the query.
218	
219	
220	EXIT STATUSES
221	=============
222	
223	0
224	: If everything goes OK.
225	
226	1
227	: If there was a network, I/O, or TLS error during operation.
228	
229	2
230	: If there is no result from the server when running in short mode. This can be any received server error, not just NXDOMAIN.
231	
232	3
233	: If there was a problem with the command-line arguments.
234	
235	4
236	: If there was a problem obtaining the system nameserver information.
237	
238	
239	AUTHOR
240	======
241	
242	dog is maintained by Benjamin ‘ogham’ Sago.
243	
244	**Website:** `https://dns.lookup.dog/` \
245	**Source code:** `https://github.com/ogham/dog`

# dog

**dog** is a command-line DNS client, like `dig`.

It has colourful output, understands normal command-line argument syntax, supports the DNS-over-TLS and DNS-over-HTTPS protocols, and can emit JSON.

![A screenshot of dog making a DNS request](dog-screenshot.png)

## Examples

    dog example.net                          Query a domain using default settings
    dog example.net MX                       ...looking up MX records instead
    dog example.net MX @1.1.1.1              ...using a specific nameserver instead
    dog example.net MX @1.1.1.1 -T           ...using TCP rather than UDP
    dog -q example.net -t MX -n 1.1.1.1 -T   As above, but using explicit arguments

## Command-line options

### Query options

    <arguments>              Human-readable host names, nameservers, types, or classes
    -q, --query=HOST         Host name or domain name to query
    -t, --type=TYPE          Type of the DNS record being queried (A, MX, NS...)
    -n, --nameserver=ADDR    Address of the nameserver to send packets to
    --class=CLASS            Network class of the DNS record being queried (IN, CH, HS)

# dog — LOC (type 29) record rendering: exhaustive reverse-engineering notes

Binary: `/workspace/executable` (dog v0.1.0). All observations made by running the binary
against a local fake DNS server (`/tmp/h/probe.py`). Probe scripts: `/tmp/explore/loc/*.py`.

Unless stated otherwise, invocations were of the form

```
dog e.net LOC -n 127.0.0.1:<port> -T --colour=never
```

with a synthetic response containing one or more type-29 answers.

---

## 1. Summary of the rendering

A LOC record's **summary string** (the "data" column of the text table, and the whole line in
`--short` mode) is:

```
{size} ({horiz_pre}, {vert_pre}) ({latitude}, {longitude}, {altitude})
```

i.e. literally

```
format!("{} ({}, {}) ({}, {}, {})", size, horiz_pre, vert_pre, latitude, longitude, altitude)
```

Baseline, byte-exact (`od -c` of the whole stdout line, `--colour=never`):

```
$ dog e.net LOC -n 127.0.0.1:PORT -T --colour=never
   rdata = 00 12 16 13 8b0d2c8c 7f3a5b40 00989680
0000000   L   O   C       e   .   n   e   t   .       5   m   0   0   s
0000020               1   e   2       (   2   2   ,       1   9   )
0000040   (   5   1 302 260   3   0 342 200 262   1   2   .   7   4   8
0000060 342 200 263       N   ,       3 302 260   3   5 342 200 262   5
0000100   2   .   7   6   8 342 200 263       W   ,       0   m   )  \n
0000120
```

python repr of the same stdout:

```python
b'LOC e.net. 5m00s   1e2 (22, 19) (51\xc2\xb030\xe2\x80\xb212.748\xe2\x80\xb3 N, 3\xc2\xb035\xe2\x80\xb252.768\xe2\x80\xb3 W, 0m)\n'
```

Exact non-ASCII characters used (confirmed with `od -c`):

| glyph | UTF-8 bytes | codepoint | name |
|---|---|---|---|
| `°` | `\302\260` = `c2 b0` | U+00B0 | DEGREE SIGN |
| `′` | `\342\200\262` = `e2 80 b2` | U+2032 | PRIME |
| `″` | `\342\200\263` = `e2 80 b3` | U+2033 | DOUBLE PRIME |

There is exactly **one ASCII space (0x20)** between the `″` and the hemisphere letter, and the
separators inside the parentheses are `", "` (comma + single space). There is a single space
between `{size}` and `(`, and between `)` and `(`. **No ANSI colour is ever emitted inside the
LOC summary** — even with `--colour=always` the summary is plain (only the type name and the
domain name of the surrounding table row are coloured).

---

## 2. Wire parsing, validation order and errors

rdata layout (16 bytes, all big-endian):

```
offset 0 : u8  version
offset 1 : u8  size          (high nibble = base, low nibble = exponent)
offset 2 : u8  horizontal precision
offset 3 : u8  vertical precision
offset 4 : u32 latitude      (milliarcseconds, biased by 2^31)
offset 8 : u32 longitude     (milliarcseconds, biased by 2^31)
offset 12: u32 altitude      (centimetres, biased by 10 000 000)
```

The rdata reader is **bounded by the RR's declared RDLENGTH**, not by the end of the packet
(proved below: declared length 0 → EOF while reading the version byte, even though 16 bytes were
physically present in the packet).

Validation order, established experimentally:

1. read `version` (1 byte) — if that read fails ⇒ `insufficient data`
2. if `version != 0` ⇒ version error (checked **before** the length check)
3. if `RDLENGTH != 16` ⇒ length error (strict equality: 15 and 17 both fail)
4. read the remaining 15 bytes — a short packet here ⇒ `insufficient data`

### 2.1 version != 0

```python
# rdata = bytes([1]) + <15 more bytes>, RDLENGTH = 16
rc  = 1
out = b''
err = b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 1, expected up to 0\n'
```

The number is the raw version byte, decimal, and "expected up to 0" is fixed:

```
version=2   -> b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 2, expected up to 0\n'
version=3   -> b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 3, expected up to 0\n'
version=5   -> b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 5, expected up to 0\n'
version=7   -> b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 7, expected up to 0\n'
version=128 -> b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 128, expected up to 0\n'
version=255 -> b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 255, expected up to 0\n'
```

The version check fires regardless of the declared length (it happens first):

```
rdata = bytes([1]),                 RDLENGTH=1  -> "record specifies version 1, expected up to 0"
rdata = bytes([1,2]),               RDLENGTH=2  -> "record specifies version 1, expected up to 0"
rdata = bytes([1])+15 good bytes,   RDLENGTH=15 -> "record specifies version 1, expected up to 0"
rdata = bytes([1])+16 good bytes,   RDLENGTH=17 -> "record specifies version 1, expected up to 0"
```

A bad LOC anywhere in the packet (answer 2 of 2, or in the additional section) aborts the whole
response — nothing at all is printed to stdout:

```
answers=[good LOC, version=3 LOC]        -> rc=1, out=b'', err="…version 3, expected up to 0\n"
answers=[good LOC], additionals=[v=7 LOC]-> rc=1, out=b'', err="…version 7, expected up to 0\n"
```

Output-mode variants of the same error:

```python

err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 1, expected up to 0\n'

# -J

out=b'{"responses":[]}\n'
err=b'{"error":true,"error_phase":"protocol","error_message":"Malformed packet: record specifies version 1, expected up to 0"}\n'

# -1 (short)
rc=2
err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record specifies version 1, expected up to 0\nNo results\n'
out=b''
```

### 2.2 wrong RDLENGTH

```
RDLENGTH=0  -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: insufficient data\n'
RDLENGTH=1  -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 1\n'
RDLENGTH=2  -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 2\n'
RDLENGTH=3  -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 3\n'
RDLENGTH=4  -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 4\n'
RDLENGTH=8  -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 8\n'
RDLENGTH=12 -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 12\n'
RDLENGTH=15 -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 15\n'
RDLENGTH=16 -> rc=0 (renders)
RDLENGTH=17 -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 17\n'
RDLENGTH=20 -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 20\n'
RDLENGTH=32 -> rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 32\n'
```

`RDLENGTH=16` declared but only 10 bytes physically present:

```
rc=1 err=b'Error [protocol]: Malformed packet: insufficient data\n'
```

JSON form of the length error:

```python
rc=1
out=b'{"responses":[]}\n'
err=b'{"error":true,"error_phase":"protocol","error_message":"Malformed packet: record length should be 16, got 15"}\n'
```

---

## 3. The `size` byte

**Rule:** `format!("{}e{}", size >> 4, size & 0x0f)` — the two nibbles printed as plain decimal
integers separated by a literal `e`. **No decoding into centimetres, no zero padding, no
validation** (base 10–15 and exponent 10–15 are accepted and printed even though RFC 1876 only
allows 0–9).

All 256 values were tested (`/tmp/explore/loc/t2_size.py`). Full mapping (`byte -> string`):

```
0x00 0e0    0x01 0e1    0x02 0e2    0x03 0e3    0x04 0e4    0x05 0e5    0x06 0e6    0x07 0e7
0x08 0e8    0x09 0e9    0x0a 0e10   0x0b 0e11   0x0c 0e12   0x0d 0e13   0x0e 0e14   0x0f 0e15
0x10 1e0    0x11 1e1    0x12 1e2    0x13 1e3    0x14 1e4    0x15 1e5    0x16 1e6    0x17 1e7
0x18 1e8    0x19 1e9    0x1a 1e10   0x1b 1e11   0x1c 1e12   0x1d 1e13   0x1e 1e14   0x1f 1e15
0x20 2e0 … 0x2f 2e15    0x30 3e0 … 0x3f 3e15    0x40 4e0 … 0x4f 4e15    0x50 5e0 … 0x5f 5e15
0x60 6e0 … 0x6f 6e15    0x70 7e0 … 0x7f 7e15    0x80 8e0 … 0x8f 8e15    0x90 9e0 … 0x9f 9e15

for every one of the 256 bytes, with zero exceptions)

0x9a -> '9e10'     0xa0 -> '10e0'    0xaf -> '10e15'   0xff -> '15e15'
```

---

## 4. Horizontal / vertical precision

**Rule:** printed **raw**, as decimal `u8` values, *not* decoded from the base/exponent
representation. Format inside the summary: `({horiz}, {vert})` — parenthesised, comma + space.

All 256 values of each byte were tested with the other pinned (`/tmp/explore/loc/t3_hpvp.py`);
every one printed as its plain decimal value, no padding, no exceptions:

```
hp=0x00 vp=0x00 -> '(0, 0)'
hp=0x01 vp=0x09 -> '(1, 9)'
hp=0x12 vp=0x12 -> '(18, 18)'
hp=0x16 vp=0x13 -> '(22, 19)'      # the RFC 1876 example bytes
hp=100  vp=200  -> '(100, 200)'
hp=0xff vp=0xff -> '(255, 255)'
```

In JSON they are emitted as **numbers**, not strings: `"precision":{"horizontal":22,"vertical":19}`.

---

## 5. Latitude and longitude

Let `d = (value as i64) - 2^31` (2147483648).

```
direction  = if d >= 0 { 'N' (lat) / 'E' (lon) } else { 'S' (lat) / 'W' (lon) }
a          = |d|                                      # milliarcseconds
limit      = 324_000_000 for latitude   (90°)
             648_000_000 for longitude  (180°)
if a > limit  -> the coordinate is None  ("Out of range" in text, null in JSON)
degrees        = a / 3_600_000
arcminutes     = (a % 3_600_000) / 60_000
arcseconds     = (a % 60_000) / 1000
milliarcseconds= a % 1000
```

Rendering:

```
if milliarcseconds == 0:
    "{degrees}°{arcminutes}′{arcseconds}″ {direction}"
else:
    "{degrees}°{arcminutes}′{arcseconds}.{milliarcseconds:03}″ {direction}"
```

Key sub-rules, each verified with many inputs:

* **Sign / hemisphere.** `d == 0` is **positive** — exactly `2^31` renders as `0°0′0″ N` for
  latitude and `0°0′0″ E` for longitude (never `S`/`W`). `d < 0` uses `S`/`W` on the *absolute*
  value, so `2^31 - 1` is `0°0′0.001″ S` / `0°0′0.001″ W` (not a negative number).
* **No zero padding on degrees / arcminutes / arcseconds.** `0°0′0″`, `1°0′0″`, `0°1′0″`,
  `89°59′59.999″`, `179°59′59.999″`, `180°0′0″`, `98°7′6.005″` (note `7′` and `6.005″`, not `07′`).
* **Fractional part.** Suppressed entirely when the milliarcsecond remainder is 0 (no `.000`,
  no trailing `.`). When non-zero it is always **exactly 3 digits, zero-padded on the left**:
  `.001`, `.007`, `.010`, `.070`, `.099`, `.100`, `.500`, `.700`, `.999`.
  All 1000 remainders 0…999 were tested exhaustively (`/tmp/explore/loc/t12_exhaustive.py`,
  0 mismatches against the rule).
* **No rounding.** The value is exact integer arithmetic on milliarcseconds; there is never a
  float involved (no `.7480000001` style artefacts, and no rounding of the 3rd decimal).
* **Range check is inclusive at the pole / antimeridian.**

```
lat = 2^31 + 324000000     -> '90°0′0″ N'
lat = 2^31 + 324000001     -> 'Out of range'
lat = 2^31 - 324000000     -> '90°0′0″ S'
lat = 2^31 - 324000001     -> 'Out of range'
lon = 2^31 + 648000000     -> '180°0′0″ E'
lon = 2^31 + 648000001     -> 'Out of range'
lon = 2^31 - 648000000     -> '180°0′0″ W'
lon = 2^31 - 648000001     -> 'Out of range'
```

* **u32 extremes.** `0`, `1`, `0xfffffffe`, `0xffffffff` are all far outside the limits for both
  coordinates and render as `Out of range`.
* **`Out of range` is per-coordinate**, exact text `Out of range` (capital O only, two spaces
  around "of"→ actually single spaces: `O u t _ o f _ r a n g e`). The rest of the summary is
  unaffected:

```python
b'LOC e.net. 5m00s   1e2 (22, 19) (Out of range, 3\xc2\xb035\xe2\x80\xb252.768\xe2\x80\xb3 W, 0m)\n'
# od -c of the summary part:
#   (   O   u   t       o   f       r   a   n   g   e   ,       3 302 260 …
b'LOC e.net. 5m00s   1e2 (22, 19) (Out of range, Out of range, 0m)\n'   # both out of range
```

Exhaustive scans that all matched the rule with zero mismatches:

* latitude degrees 0…90 N and 0…90 S (182 records)
* longitude degrees 0…180 E and 0…180 W (362 records)
* arcminutes 0…59, arcseconds 0…59
* milliarcseconds 0…999 (1000 records)
* 240 uniformly random `(lat, lon, alt, size, hp, vp)` tuples, half of them with fully random u32
  latitudes/longitudes (i.e. mostly out of range)

---

## 6. Altitude

Let `d = (alt as i64) - 10_000_000` (the RFC 1876 datum, i.e. 100 000 m below sea level in
centimetres). Then, using **truncating (toward-zero) integer division and a remainder that keeps
the sign of the dividend** (Rust `/` and `%` on `i64`):

```
metres      = d / 100
centimetres = d % 100
if centimetres == 0:  "{metres}m"
else:                 "{metres}.{centimetres:02}m"
```

The unit string is a bare lowercase `m` appended with **no space**.

### 6.1 The negative-remainder bug (important!)

Because the remainder keeps the sign of `d`, **negative altitudes with a non-zero centimetre part
print a minus sign after the decimal point.** This is reproducible and must be replicated exactly:

```
alt = 9999999  (d = -1)        -> '0.-1m'
alt = 9999950  (d = -50)       -> '0.-50m'
alt = 9999901  (d = -99)       -> '0.-99m'
alt = 9999900  (d = -100)      -> '-1m'
alt = 9999899  (d = -101)      -> '-1.-1m'
alt = 9999801  (d = -199)      -> '-1.-99m'
alt = 9999800  (d = -200)      -> '-2m'
alt = 9999750  (d = -250)      -> '-2.-50m'
alt = 9876544  (d = -123456)   -> '-1234.-56m'
alt = 99       (d = -9999901)  -> '-99999.-1m'
alt = 1        (d = -9999999)  -> '-99999.-99m'
alt = 0        (d = -10000000) -> '-100000m'
alt = 100      (d = -9999900)  -> '-99999m'
```

Note also that the integral part is `0` (never `-0`) when `-100 < d < 0`.

The `{:02}` width includes the sign, Rust-style: `-1` → `"-1"` (already 2 chars, no zero
inserted), `-50` → `"-50"`, whereas positive `1` → `"01"` and `9` → `"09"`.

### 6.2 Positive side

```
alt = 10000000 (d = 0)         -> '0m'
alt = 10000001 (d = +1)        -> '0.01m'
alt = 10000009 (d = +9)        -> '0.09m'
alt = 10000010 (d = +10)       -> '0.10m'
alt = 10000050 (d = +50)       -> '0.50m'
alt = 10000099 (d = +99)       -> '0.99m'
alt = 10000100 (d = +100)      -> '1m'
alt = 10000250 (d = +250)      -> '2.50m'
alt = 10001000 (d = +1000)     -> '10m'
alt = 10100000 (d = +100000)   -> '1000m'
alt = 10123456 (d = +123456)   -> '1234.56m'
alt = 14200000 (d = +4200000)  -> '42000m'
alt = 20000000                 -> '100000m'
alt = 1000000000               -> '9900000m'
alt = 2147483647 (i32 max)     -> '21374836.47m'
alt = 2147483648 (2^31)        -> '21374836.48m'
alt = 3000000000               -> '29900000m'
alt = 4200000000               -> '41900000m'
alt = 4294967200               -> '42849672m'
alt = 4294967294               -> '42849672.94m'
alt = 4294967295 (u32 max)     -> '42849672.95m'
```

`4294967295 - 10000000 = 4284967295` exceeds `i32::MAX`, so the arithmetic is done in at least
64 bits (or the value is widened before subtraction). Altitude is **never** "Out of range" —
every one of the u32 values probed rendered.

All 501 altitudes in `[10000000-250, 10000000+250]` were tested exhaustively — 0 mismatches
against the rule above.

---

## 7. JSON output (`-J`)

The LOC `data` object, key order fixed, compact separators (`,` and `:`, no spaces):

```json
{"size":"1e2","precision":{"horizontal":22,"vertical":19},"point":{"latitude":"51°30′12.748″ N","longitude":"3°35′52.768″ W","altitude":"0m"}}
```

Rules:

* `size` — **string**, exactly the same `"{base}e{exp}"` text as the table.
* `precision.horizontal`, `precision.vertical` — **numbers** (0…255).
* `point.latitude`, `point.longitude` — **string** with the same `D°M′S[.mmm]″ H` text as the
  table, **or JSON `null`** when the coordinate is out of range (never the string
  `"Out of range"`).
* `point.altitude` — **string** with the same text as the table, including the `-1234.-56m`
  bug forms.
* The `°`, `′`, `″` characters are emitted as **raw UTF-8**, *not* `°` escapes.

Literal captures:

## 8. Integration with the text table

The LOC summary is the last column of the standard dog row:

```
{type:>3} {name:<W} {ttl:>T} {section_marker} {summary}
```

Observed (`--colour=never`), answers/authority/additional in one packet, names `e.net.`,
`ns.e.net.`, `ad.e.net.`, TTLs 300/60/7200:

```python
b'LOC e.net.       5m00s   1e2 (22, 19) (51\xc2\xb030\xe2\x80\xb212.748\xe2\x80\xb3 N, 3\xc2\xb035\xe2\x80\xb252.768\xe2\x80\xb3 W, 0m)\n'
b'LOC ns.e.net.    1m00s A 2e1 (22, 19) (51\xc2\xb030\xe2\x80\xb212.748\xe2\x80\xb3 N, 3\xc2\xb035\xe2\x80\xb252.768\xe2\x80\xb3 W, 1.23m)\n'
b'LOC ad.e.net. 2h00m00s + 3e5 (22, 19) (0\xc2\xb00\xe2\x80\xb20\xe2\x80\xb3 N, 0\xc2\xb00\xe2\x80\xb20\xe2\x80\xb3 E, -100000m)\n'
```

* type column right-aligned to the widest type name (`  A` next to `LOC`/`TXT`)
* name column left-aligned to the widest name
* TTL column right-aligned to the widest formatted TTL
* section marker: `' '` for answers, `'A'` for authority, `'+'` for additional; one space either
  side of it. With a single answer this collapses to the familiar three spaces:
  `'5m00s' + ' ' + ' ' + ' ' + '1e2'` = `5m00s   1e2`.
* no trailing whitespace after the summary; line terminated by a single `\n`

With `--colour=always` the LOC row is:

```python

so: type name in `ESC[33m` … `ESC[0m` (yellow), domain in `ESC[1;34m` … `ESC[0m` (bold blue),
authority marker `A` in `ESC[36m`, additional marker `+` in `ESC[32m`, **and nothing inside the
LOC summary is coloured**.

`--short` / `-1` prints only the summary of each answer (one per line), no colour codes:

```python

`--seconds` and `--time` do not change the LOC summary at all (they only affect the TTL column /
add a trailing `Ran in 0ms` line). Class `CH` / unknown class 99 do not change LOC parsing.

## 10. Reference implementation (python, byte-exact against everything probed)

```python
EQ = 2**31
DATUM = 10_000_000

def size_str(b: int) -> str:
    return "%de%d" % (b >> 4, b & 0x0f)

def coord(v: int, pos: str, neg: str, limit: int):
    d = v - EQ
    direction = pos if d >= 0 else neg
    a = abs(d)
    if a > limit:
        return None                      # -> "Out of range" / JSON null
    deg, rem = divmod(a, 3_600_000)
    mins, rem = divmod(rem, 60_000)
    sec, mas  = divmod(rem, 1000)
    s = ("%d.%03d" % (sec, mas)) if mas else ("%d" % sec)
    return "%d°%d′%s″ %s" % (deg, mins, s, direction)

def alt_str(a: int) -> str:
    d = a - DATUM
    m  = int(d / 100) if d >= 0 else -((-d) // 100)   # truncate toward zero
    cm = d - m * 100                                  # sign follows d
    if cm == 0:
        return "%dm" % m
    frac = ("%02d" % cm) if cm >= 0 else str(cm)      # Rust "{:02}" incl. sign
    return "%d.%sm" % (m, frac)

def loc_summary(size, hp, vp, lat, lon, alt) -> str:
    la = coord(lat, 'N', 'S', 324_000_000) or "Out of range"
    lo = coord(lon, 'E', 'W', 648_000_000) or "Out of range"
    return "%s (%d, %d) (%s, %s, %s)" % (size_str(size), hp, vp, la, lo, alt_str(alt))
```

This model was differentially tested against the binary on **261 table cases** and **180 JSON
cases** of mixed edge/random inputs plus the exhaustive scans in §3–§6: **zero mismatches**.

## 13. Things that could NOT be determined

* Whether the internal integer type for the coordinate arithmetic is `i64`, `i32` or `f64` —
  every observable output is consistent with exact integer arithmetic on `i64`, and the
  milliarcsecond values can never overflow `i32` after the `- 2^31` bias, so the choice is not
  observable. (Altitude *is* observably at least 64-bit, since `4294967295 - 10000000` exceeds
  `i32::MAX` and renders correctly.)
* Whether the range check is implemented as `abs(d) > limit` on the raw milliarcseconds or as a
  post-decomposition check (`degrees > 90`, or `degrees == 90 && (min|sec|mas) != 0`). Both are
  behaviourally identical for all 2^32 inputs, so the distinction is unobservable.
* Whether `Out of range` comes from the `Display` impl of the record or from the table renderer
  substituting for `None`. The JSON emits `null` and the table emits `Out of range`, so the string
  is at least not shared with the JSON serialiser; which layer owns it is not observable.
* The exact `size`-byte formatting used in the trace log (`0b010010` for `0x12` is consistent with
  Rust `{:#08b}`, but `{:#08b}` vs `{:#06b}`+prefix accounting cannot be distinguished for values
  ≥ `0x40`; both give the observed strings — this only affects trace output, not the record
  rendering).
* No LOC-specific behaviour was observed for `--edns`, `-Z` tweaks, `--txid`, DoT/DoH transports,
  or non-IN classes; they were spot-checked (class `CH`, class 99, `--seconds`, `--time`,
  `--colour=always`, UDP vs TCP) and none altered the LOC summary bytes, but the DoT/DoH
  transports could not be exercised at all in this sandbox (no TLS server available).
* Whether dog would ever render a LOC record from a *cached/hints* source (e.g. `/etc/hosts`
  hints are read at startup) — not reachable for type 29.
